newsitem.title: USA: U.S. jury weighs life or death for McVeigh.
newsitem.headline: U.S. jury weighs life or death for McVeigh.

text.p: Jurors began weighing life or death for Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh on Thursday after hearing a final plea from prosecutors who urged them to tell McVeigh he was a traitor who deserved to die.
"Look into the eyes of a coward and tell him you will have courage," prosecutor Beth Wilkinson said. "Tell him he is no patriot. He is a traitor and he deserves to die."

"It's time, it's time for justice," she told the jury of seven men and five women who 10 days ago found McVeigh guilty of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, killing 168 people in the worst mass murder in U.S. history.
The jury must choose between death by lethal injection for McVeigh or life in prison without possibility of parole.
For the first time, chief defence attorney Stephen Jones did not dispute McVeigh's guilt. "He is not a demon, though surely his act was demonic," he said.
But he urged the jury to spare McVeigh's life, suggesting that if he died the full story of the April 19, 1995 bombing may never be known and other possible conspirators never brought to justice.
"Dead men do not tell tales. The government may not be the only people who want my client executed," Jones said, implying others would like to see McVeigh take his secret to the grave.
"The book of the Oklahoma City bombing is not closed ... Do not close it. Do not permit others to close it. Let there be a full accounting," he said as McVeigh looked on stern-faced.
Jones has suggested throughout that other people were involved in the bomb plot, at one point saying the real bomber may have died in the blast.

In his rebuttal statement, chief prosecutor Joe Hartzler told the jury he regretted having to ask them to send a man to his death. "I'm sorry to have to ask you to do this. I'm sorry you have to do it, but you do," he said in a hushed voice to the solemn jury.

After instructing the jurors on the fine points of the law for 30 minutes, federal Judge Richard Matsch sent the jurors off to begin deliberations. "The law requires you to approach the sentencing decision with an open mind," Matsch said.
He did not sequester them as he had during earlier deliberations on whether McVeigh was guilty or not.

Before leaving the courtroom, McVeigh looked at his mother Mildred Frazer, who was in court with his father Bill and sister Jennifer. His mother waved to McVeigh and he nodded back before being escorted out by U.S. marshals.
The jury began deliberating with the final impassioned appeal of the lawyers ringing in their ears.
In a powerful speech, Wilkinson stressed the enormity of McVeigh's crime, saying the April 19, 1995 attack was "the most bloody domestic terrorist act in the history of our country."

Wilkinson said McVeigh, a 29-year-old ex-soldier, killed more Americans on a single day than were killed in combat in the Gulf War. "There would not be enough seats in this courtroom if we could bring them all back today," she said.

"We never knew such a dark and horrible place existed in America until Timothy McVeigh sent us there ... It is time for justice, it is time to impose the ultimate sanction on the man responsible for this terror ... Sentence Timothy McVeigh to death," she urged the jury.

But the defence urged the jury to spare McVeigh's life, saying all Americans were partly to blame for the Oklahoma City bombing because the country failed to respond adequately to federal sieges at Ruby Ridge, Idaho in 1992 and at Waco, Texas in 1993 that became rallying cries for the right-wing.
"We should not feel a clear conscience. We all bear some responsibility for Oklahoma City," defence attorney Richard Burr said.

The defence has said McVeigh was deeply disturbed by the deaths of 80 Branch Davidian cult members in a confrontation with federal agents at Waco. Prosecutors said he bombed the Murrah building to avenge their deaths.
McVeigh was found guilty June 2 of 11 murder, conspiracy and bombing charges, all carrying a possible death penalty.
